ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All participants read an identical description of mild CSM and were randomized to one of three scenarios: surgery that improved symptoms, surgery that halted progression without improvement, or nonoperative management with symptom progression.
Many participants were undecided (4% to 36% in the surgical scenarios, 27% to 43% in the nonoperative scenario).
Respondents were recruited through CloudResearch Prime Panels over a 1-week period between 14 and 20 May 2026.
After consent, participants were randomized 1:1:1 to one of three scenarios.

Further, for most complications resolving within three months, more participants were undecided than would change their treatment choice; the only exception was difficulty swallowing at 3 months in Scenario 1 (Supplementary Table S2, Panel A).
table.formatted: Further, for most complications resolving within three months, more participants were undecided than would change their treatment choice; the only exception was difficulty swallowing at 3 months in Scenario 1 (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>, Panel A).
table.header: Effect of the Described Duration of a Complication

table.text: In this randomized experiment, participants were asked to imagine that they had mild CSM and to consider whether they would choose or avoid surgery after a specific adverse outcome.
Participants were members of the public asked to imagine a diagnosis, so their responses indicate hypothetical stated preferences rather than actual treatment decisions.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> All participants read an identical description of mild CSM and were randomized to one of three scenarios: surgery that improved symptoms, surgery that halted progression without improvement, or nonoperative management with symptom progression.

> Many participants were undecided (4% to 36% in the surgical scenarios, 27% to 43% in the nonoperative scenario).

> Respondents were recruited through CloudResearch Prime Panels over a 1-week period between 14 and 20 May 2026.

> After consent, participants were randomized 1:1:1 to one of three scenarios.

> Further, for most complications resolving within three months, more participants were undecided than would change their treatment choice; the only exception was difficulty swallowing at 3 months in Scenario 1 (Supplementary Table S2, Panel A).

> In this randomized experiment, participants were asked to imagine that they had mild CSM and to consider whether they would choose or avoid surgery after a specific adverse outcome.

> Participants were members of the public asked to imagine a diagnosis, so their responses indicate hypothetical stated preferences rather than actual treatment decisions.

Ethics approval statement:

> Louis Human Research Protection Office (IRB #202511100).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_exact.title: Exact P-Values
stat_p_exact.summary_text: We found 1 imprecise *p* value out of 5 detected *p* values.

table.formatted: Mean ratings were higher in Scenario 2 for all twelve complications (exact sign test p < 0.001), but the differences were small, ranging from 0.45 to 1.44 points on the 0-10 scale.
table.expanded: Mean ratings were higher in Scenario 2 for all twelve complications (exact sign test p < 0.001), but the differences were small, ranging from 0.45 to 1.44 points on the 0-10 scale.

table.formatted: Seven of the twelve comparisons had p < 0.05 before adjustment for multiple comparisons.
table.expanded: Seven of the twelve comparisons had p < 0.05 before adjustment for multiple comparisons.

table.formatted: The largest difference was for transient shoulder weakness, whose median rose from 5 (IQR 3-7) to 7 (5-9) (p < 0.001).
table.expanded: The largest difference was for transient shoulder weakness, whose median rose from 5 (IQR 3-7) to 7 (5-9) (p < 0.001).

table.formatted: The undecided proportion differed significantly between scenarios for one complication only: new neck pain persisting at one year, from 14.6% in Scenario 1 to 4.4% in Scenario 2 (p = 0.023) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>; Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>, Panel A).
table.header: Dominant Decision Factors: Factors Influencing Surgery vs. Nonoperative Management
table.expanded: The undecided proportion differed significantly between scenarios for one complication only: new neck pain persisting at one year, from 14.6% in Scenario 1 to 4.4% in Scenario 2 (p = 0.023) (Figure 1; Supplementary Table S2, Panel A).
Participants with Medicaid coverage (n=20) rated a smaller proportion of complications as dominant factors than participants with private insurance, a difference of 15.0 percentage points (p = 0.03).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < 0.05", Text = "Seven of the twelve comparisons had p < 0.05 before adjustment for multiple comparisons."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::
